lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.introduction: An array stores a fixed-size list of values of the same data type under a single name — ideal for LED banks and multi-sensor readings.
objectives: Declare and initialize fixed-size C++ arrays.
Explain why all elements in an array share one data type.
Store multiple pin numbers cleanly in one array.
conceptExplanation: Instead of declaring led1, led2, led3, led4, led5 as five separate variables, an array groups them into one contiguous block of SRAM: const int LEDS[4] = {8, 9, 10, 11};.
Arrays pair naturally with for loops so you can configure or update 4 or 40 pins with just three lines of code.
lessons.analogy: An array is a pill organizer with numbered compartments in a row — every slot holds the same kind of item and is accessed by slot number.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Specify element type, array name, size in brackets [ ], and brace-enclosed values.
rules: Array size is fixed at compile time.
All elements must share the same data type.

codeExamples.title: LED Pin Array
codeExamples.description: Stores four LED pins in a single array.

lineByLine.explanation: Creates a 4-element integer array of pin numbers.
Configures each pin using index i.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Line-following robots store their 5 or 8 IR reflectance sensor pins and readings inside arrays.

commonMistakes.fix: Valid indices for size 4 are 0, 1, 2, and 3 only.

tryItYourself.title: m07_arrays.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add pin 12 as a 5th element and update the array size and loop limit to 5.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Configures all 5 digital pins (8 through 12) as OUTPUT cleanly.

exercises.prompt: What is the valid index range for `int samples[5];`?
exercises.explanation: C++ arrays are zero-indexed, so a 5-element array uses indices 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4.

exercises.prompt: Declare an array of 3 ints named pins.
exercises.explanation: The bracket size matches the 3 initializer values.

summary: Arrays store multiple values of one type in contiguous memory.
Indices always start at 0 and end at size - 1.
Arrays eliminate repetitive pin declarations.

lessons.title: Indexing
lessons.introduction: Indexing reads or updates a specific slot inside an array using square brackets [index], starting from 0.
objectives: Read and modify individual array elements by index.
Avoid out-of-bounds memory corruption on Arduino.
conceptExplanation: The first item in an array is ALWAYS at index 0, and the last item is at index (length - 1). Because C++ does not perform automatic bounds checking, reading or writing past the end of an array silently corrupts adjacent SRAM variables!
lessons.analogy: Like European building floors where the ground floor is 0, array indexing starts at 0.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Use arrayName[index] to read or assign a specific element.
rules: Never access index < 0 or index >= arraySize.

codeExamples.title: Reading & Updating Array Slots
codeExamples.description: Modifies index 1 and prints elements 0 and 1.

lineByLine.explanation: Updates the SECOND element (index 1) from 150 to 180.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Lookup tables store pre-calibrated servo angles indexed by gripper preset number.

commonMistakes.fix: Index 3 is out of bounds and corrupts SRAM! Last valid index is 2.

tryItYourself.title: m07_indexing.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Print the last element (speeds[2]) as well.

summary: Array indexing starts at 0.
Use array[i] to read or overwrite a slot.
Out-of-bounds indexing corrupts microcontroller SRAM.

lessons.title: Iterating Through Arrays
lessons.introduction: Combining a for loop with an array lets you process every sensor channel or LED in just a few lines.
objectives: Compute array length safely using sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]).
Iterate through an array to sum, average, or drive outputs.
conceptExplanation: Using sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]) automatically calculates the element count so you never forget to update loop limits when adding another LED or sensor.
lessons.analogy: Walking down a row of mailboxes inspecting each one in order from 0 to N-1.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Compute count with sizeof and loop from i = 0 while i < count.
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
const int N = sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]);
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) { ... }
rules: Always use strictly less-than (i < N) to stay inside bounds.

codeExamples.title: Computing Average of Sensor Array

lineByLine.explanation: Computes element count (5) safely regardless of int byte size.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Moving-average filters keep the last N distance readings in an array and iterate to compute a smooth average.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using sizeof(samples) directly as the element count
commonMistakes.fix: sizeof returns BYTES, not elements! Divide by sizeof(samples[0]).

tryItYourself.title: m07_iterate.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a 6th reading (25) to samples[] and notice how sizeof adapts automatically.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints the exact decimal average of all array elements.

exercises.prompt: Which expression returns the number of elements in an int array named data?
exercises.explanation: Dividing total array bytes by one element's byte size gives exact element count.

summary: Use for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) to traverse arrays.
Calculate element count with sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]).
Pair float casting with sums for accurate averages.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.introduction: Arduino's String object makes text formatting convenient, while requiring awareness of heap fragmentation on small AVR boards.
objectives: Create, concatenate, and compare Arduino String objects.
Understand when String is fine vs when fixed char arrays are safer.
conceptExplanation: The Arduino String class lets you join text with +, check .length(), and compare with ==. On 32-bit boards (Uno R4, ESP32) with lots of RAM, String is very comfortable; on 2 KB SRAM boards (Uno R3 / Nano Classic), avoid repeatedly building huge Strings inside loop().
lessons.analogy: A String object is an expandable binder that dynamically resizes itself, convenient but requiring extra shelf space.

rules: Use String for readable Serial logs, but keep repeated loop() concatenation minimal on Uno R3.

codeExamples.title: Formatting Telemetry with String

lineByLine.explanation: Converts integer 88 into text so it can be joined with +.

lessons.realWorldApplication: ESP32 Wi-Fi dashboards and LCD status lines format human-readable labels using Strings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Heavy String concatenation inside a fast loop() on Uno R3
commonMistakes.fix: Print pieces directly with separate Serial.print() calls to avoid SRAM fragmentation.

tryItYourself.title: m07_strings.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change robotName to your own robot's name.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints the formatted battery telemetry line to Serial Monitor.

exercises.prompt: Why should you be cautious with frequent String concatenation inside loop() on an Arduino Uno R3?
options: Uno R3 only has 2 KB of SRAM, and dynamic String resizing can fragment heap memory.
String does not exist on Arduino.
exercises.explanation: Dynamic heap allocations in 2 KB SRAM can cause crashes over long uptimes.

summary: String objects support +, ==, and .length().
On Uno R3/Nano Classic, prefer multiple Serial.print() calls or char arrays for long-running loops.

lessons.title: Character Arrays (C-Strings)
lessons.introduction: Null-terminated char arrays (C-strings) store text in fixed, predictable memory with zero heap fragmentation.
objectives: Compare C-strings using strcmp() instead of ==.
conceptExplanation: In standard C++, a C-string is simply a char array ending with the invisible null character '\0'. Because its size is fixed at compile time, it never fragments SRAM — making it the gold standard for reliable embedded firmware.
lessons.analogy: A fixed nameplate with an end-stop marker ('\0') telling Serial.print where the text finishes.

rules: Reserve 1 extra byte for the trailing '\0' terminator.
Always compare C-strings with strcmp(a, b) == 0, never a == b.

codeExamples.title: Comparing C-Strings Safely
codeExamples.description: Uses strcmp() to match a command buffer.

lineByLine.explanation: Returns 0 when both C-strings contain identical characters.

lessons.realWorldApplication: GPS NMEA sentence parsers and Serial protocol handlers on AVR boards use char buffers for rock-solid uptime.

commonMistakes.fix: That compares memory addresses, not text! Always use strcmp(cmd, "STOP") == 0.

tryItYourself.title: m07_cstrings.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change cmd to "GO" and add an else branch printing "Running".

exercises.prompt: What value does strcmp(a, b) return when two C-strings are identical?
exercises.explanation: strcmp returns 0 when there is zero difference between the two strings.

summary: C-strings are char arrays terminated by '\0'.
They avoid heap fragmentation on low-RAM boards.
Compare C-strings with strcmp(a, b) == 0.

lessons.title: Structures (struct)
lessons.introduction: A struct bundles related variables of different data types (like pin, threshold, and reading) into a single custom record.
objectives: Define a struct grouping mixed fields.
Access struct members using the dot (.) operator.
conceptExplanation: Arrays hold many items of the SAME type; a struct holds related properties of DIFFERENT types — for instance, a SensorNode struct holding an int pin, float distanceCm, and bool alertActive.
lessons.analogy: A contact card that groups Name (text), Age (int), and Active (bool) into one tidy package.

syntaxExplanation.summary: struct TypeName { fields... }; followed by a semicolon.
rules: Never forget the semicolon ';' after the closing brace of a struct definition.
Access fields with dot notation: data.voltage.

codeExamples.title: SensorData Struct
codeExamples.description: Groups raw ADC, voltage, and alert status into one struct.

lineByLine.explanation: Reads the volts field using dot notation.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Telemetry packets sent over LoRa or Wi-Fi bundle GPS latitude, longitude, altitude, and battery voltage into a single struct.

commonMistakes.fix: C++ requires ';' immediately after the struct's closing brace.

tryItYourself.title: m07_struct.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change battery.warning to false and observe the output.

exercises.prompt: Access the volts member of the struct variable sensor.
exercises.explanation: The dot operator (.) accesses members of a struct.

summary: struct groups related fields of different types into one custom type.
End struct definitions with a semicolon ';'.
Use dot notation (item.field) to read or write members.

lessons.title: Enumerations (enum)
lessons.introduction: An enum replaces cryptic state numbers (0, 1, 2) with readable names like STATE_IDLE, STATE_DRIVE, and STATE_AVOID.
objectives: Define an enum for robot operating states.
Combine enum with switch for clean state machines.
conceptExplanation: Instead of remembering whether mode 2 means 'Turning' or 'Alarm', an enum gives each integer state a descriptive identifier that the compiler checks for typos.
lessons.analogy: Traffic light labels RED, YELLOW, GREEN instead of secret codes 0, 1, 2.

syntaxExplanation.pattern:
enum RobotState { IDLE, DRIVE, AVOID };
RobotState state = DRIVE;

codeExamples.title: Readable Robot State Machine with enum
codeExamples.description: Uses enum values inside a switch statement.

lineByLine.explanation: Dispatches cleanly on readable state names.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Almost every autonomous robot firmware uses an enum-driven Finite State Machine (FSM) to manage navigation modes.

commonMistakes.fix: Just like struct, enum definitions end with ';'.

tryItYourself.title: m07_enum.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change currentState to AVOID and check which message prints.

exercises.prompt: Why is an enum preferred over raw numbers 0, 1, 2 for robot states?
options: Named states make code self-documenting and prevent typos.
exercises.explanation: Readable names like AVOID or IDLE make state machines far easier to maintain.

summary: enum defines a named set of integer constants.
Ideal for Finite State Machines (FSMs) paired with switch.
Always end an enum definition with a semicolon.
